# Afterword {.unnumbered}

The 1446 book closed with a postface, and it made two claims for its little
alphabet. The first was that a wise man could learn it before the morning was
over, and a slow one within ten days. The second was that it could write down
any sound at all: the wind, the cry of a crane, the crowing of a cock, the
barking of a dog. This book closes by restating both, because they are its own
measures of success.

## The ten-day challenge

The first claim was about speed, and [the
preface](index.qmd#the-promise-and-the-books-rules) restated it for this book:
read the whole grammar in a morning, and write it fluently within ten days. You
have done the reading. Here is the rest of the promise. For the next ten days,
ask one question a day of *your own data*, not of the book's cast of tables,
and answer it in one sentence. Start where the [cookbook](parts/cookbook.qmd)
starts: with your columns and your question. By day three the recipes will read
as ordinary sentences, because you will have written sentences like them
yourself. By day ten you should be writing sentences this book never showed
you. That is the one outcome that proves you learned the grammar and not the
examples.

During those ten days,
[report](https://github.com/psychometrician/gog/issues) two kinds of result: a
sentence that renders when you expected a refusal, and a refusal whose
direction you disagree with. Reports like these are how the grammar's mistakes
are found.

## Growth without new words

The second claim was about what the letters could write: any sound at all. gog
has the same goal for plots, but it does not promise that every plot is
possible. The kernel you learned is its whole vocabulary. The engine draws every
word in it, though not every *pairing* of words.
[Combinations](combinations.qmd) shows which pairs it draws and which it
refuses.

A new kind of plot does not need a new word. The **choropleth** is an example
of that. It is a map that shades each country by a value, and no atom was added
for it. What it needed was a different kind of table: one row for every point
along a country's border, so that many rows make up one country. A `zone` is a
filled region, and several things can decide its sides. One of them is a
**boundary**, the outline those rows trace, and `group` already says which rows
belong to one country. [Map](map.qmd) shows the choropleth drawn with the words
the kernel already had.

The vocabulary is also the same in all four languages. Whatever sentence you
write, all four bindings build the same specification from its words. The main
difference is how each binding names a column. JavaScript also cannot give the
operators new meanings, so it spells them as words. Each language has a chapter
of its own, listing what differs: [R](bindings/r.qmd),
[Python](bindings/python.qmd), [Julia](bindings/julia.qmd),
[JavaScript](bindings/javascript.qmd). Here is one sentence from [A first
plot](first-plot.qmd) in all four:

```r
# R
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)
```

```python
# Python
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)
  + color(col.continent))
```

```julia
# Julia
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)
```

```js
// JavaScript
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), color(col.continent))
```

All four draw the same plot, byte for byte.

## One goal left

Those four spellings are finished work. One thing this project planned to do is
not finished, and it is written down here so you can check later whether the
project did it. Half of it already works: the engine itself runs inside the
page, which is how a 3-D plot turns when you drag it in the web edition. The
other half is making every example in this book editable on the page. You could
then change `color(continent)` to `shape(continent)` and watch the plot redraw.
This book is ready for editable examples, because no plot in it is a
screenshot: the engine draws every one from its specification.

## Writing quickly is not writing well

Both claims of 1446 are about the letters: how fast they can be learned, and
what they can write. Neither says how well anyone will write with them.

I think Hangeul (한글) is the best writing system in the world. I should admit
that I may be biased, because it is the alphabet I write with. Most people
agree that it is quick to learn, to read and to write.

Writing quickly is not the same as writing well. Good writing cannot be learned
quickly: you read good writing, and you practice. Visualization is no
different. This tool is new and still has problems, but I hope it is already a
good tool to practice with.

The 1446 story makes the same distinction, between making a writing system and
writing with it. King Sejong made the alphabet. Other people wrote most of the
books that used it. I designed gog, but I am not a great author of plots. What
I do have is twenty years as a user of visualization tools, watching and
listening and reading. The design comes from that experience, and the result is
a tool that is easy to learn and easy to use.

I hope you do good work with it.

## The gap

A specification is a sentence written before the picture exists. Between
writing it and the moment the engine shows you what you said, there is a gap,
and everyone who writes a specification waits in it. The package is `gog`. The
state you are in while you wait is *agog*: eager to see what comes next. I hope
the book kept you agog.
